prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing frequency standards to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clearly defined invention (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, proposed by Katori) followed by a decisive realization at record accuracy and stability (Ye's group), with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. Independent laboratories on several continents reproduce and now routinely compare these clocks, so the physics is settled rather than interpretive. The consequences are concrete: a pending redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. Attribution fits two names without strain, which is rare on this shortlist. Seven of eight opening ballots rank it, five in the top three, and after reading the arguments I find the reasoning behind that support stronger than the case I put forward for my own first choice. I rank it first on the merits of maturity, clarity of credit and a discovery-grade measurement advance, not because many colleagues ranked it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is subject overlap with earlier prizes: the 2005 frequency-comb award and the 2012 award for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks both sit close to this territory, so the committee may feel precision metrology has recently been honoured. The practical payoff is also partly prospective, since the redefinition of the second has not happened, and other lattice-clock groups (strontium and ytterbium efforts in Paris, PTB and elsewhere) and ultrastable-laser developers are not credited. If the committee judges the clock itself an engineering refinement of known atomic physics, B014 offers a more conceptual theory-plus-experiment story, at the cost of a younger field with an unresolved superconducting mechanism.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first because measurement-limited progress is central to physics, the invention is original, and multiple laboratories have reproduced and surpassed the first results, so the timing is not premature.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the two-name attribution. Where I qualify it is the grouping question he raises himself: if ultrastable-laser or comb work is folded in, the allocation changes and the 2005 prize overlap becomes real. I think the citation should stay tight on the magic-wavelength lattice clock itself, with Katori for the concept and Ye for the performance and systematics, and not stretch into general laser stabilization. Read that way, I am persuaded that this is distinct from comb and ion-clock recognition.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B005 first and argues that the conceptual step is clean, the contribution is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and independent confirmation is extensive across strontium and ytterbium. She also ranks circuit QED seventh partly because of the 2025 prize.
responses.response: On B005 I accept her distinctness argument and drop my earlier lower placement. On circuit QED I take her proximity point seriously and partly concede it. My own first choice rested on a field I know well, and the 2025 award for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits is a real reason for a gap, even though cQED is a separate discovery. I would not argue that the 2025 prize duplicates it, but the credit gap around Wallraff and Devoret is a second reason the three-name list is weak. I now treat B046 as a later candidate and not a lead.

responses.point: Mehlig places twisted bilayer graphene second with MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as the core pair, regards Bistritzer as a junior third name, and notes some may see the field as slightly early; he ranks lattice clocks third.
responses.response: I share his view that the decisive pairing is MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero and that the origin of superconductivity is still debated, which is why I keep B014 as an alternative and not my preferred prize. We disagree on weight: he sees maturity as high for both, but eight years of moire work, with the central phase diagram still moving, is a shorter record than two decades of lattice clocks. If B014 is chosen I would credit the pair, or the trio only if the committee judges the 2011 continuum model to be a joint result.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing the prediction-then-discovery sequence is decisive, reproduction is broad, and recognition is timely and not premature, while he ranks lattice clocks sixth because the SI redefinition is pending.
responses.response: His timing argument for B014 is fair and I do not think it is premature enough to exclude it. I do not accept his reservation about clocks, though. A pending redefinition is a use of the invention, not a condition for its validity, and the performance has already been confirmed in many national laboratories. By contrast, the theory attribution in B014 remains open (Lopes dos Santos and others, Cao as lead author), so I find the clock credit cleaner.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see lattice clocks as too close to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the redefinition of the second, if it occurs soon, strengthens the case or merely shows it is already settled.
Whether other lattice-clock groups should weigh against a two-name credit; my knowledge of early priority between the Tokyo and Boulder efforts is from memory and not verified here.
If B014 is preferred by colleagues, whether Bistritzer belongs beside MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work in superconducting circuits and quantum computing, so B046 (circuit QED) and, less directly, B024 and B015 (quantum-computing and simulation theory) are close to my own field; I should not be the one to press B046 and would consider recusal on it. Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and co-author Anton Frisk Kockum are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer is apparent from the provided profile.
